answer: Agents can earn influence only through repeated trades that counterparties later attest were fulfilled; each attestation is weighted by the counterparty’s own history, not by the number of identities it controls. A new identity starts with no trusted weight, so an attacker cannot cheaply multiply votes by minting accounts: it must acquire scarce goods or services, complete real transactions, and persuade established agents to risk their reputation by vouching. A sparrow trading from a ledge to a wharf still needs that costly history.
